## Overview

-   Often have a large number of variables included in an observational dataset

-   We have discussed various methods to estimate the causal effect which rely on fitting regression models without a lot of discussion on which variables to include or not include

-   The only thing that we have definitively stated is that $X$ needs to ensure that that $\{Y^1, Y^0\}$ are independent of $A$ conditioned on $X$

## DAGs

-   In some applications it makes sense to draw the causal structure/relationship among variables (regardless of whether they are measured)
-   Arrows point in the direction of causal effect
-   Known as a directed acyclic graph (“Directed:” edges imply a direction. “Acyclic:” no cycles, a variable cannot cause itself, either directly or through another variable.)

## DAGs

-   There is a lot of theory relating probability theory (conditional independence) to DAGs with some unusual terms (d-separation, collider, etc.)
-   In particular, IF you have drawn the correct DAG, DAG will tell you which variables you would need to adjust for (causal reasoning) and which you should not
-   In my experience, can spend a lot of time learning the "rules" of DAGs without a lot of benefit

## Causal Discovery

-   Ongoing work to be able to learn the DAG from just data alone
-   May not represent causal relationships without additional assumptions

## Some Simple Rules

To understand causal effect of $A$ on $Y$

-   Never adjust for variables which come after treatment decision or when randomization would have occurred. These are (intermediate) outcomes
-   Do not care about the relationship between pre-treatment variables
-   This leaves four types of variables

1)  Common causes of $A$ and $Y$
2)  Causes of $Y$ alone
3)  Causes of $A$ alone
4)  Causes of neither $A$ or $Y$

## Causal Inference: Target Trial

-   Throughout the course we have thought about trying to use analytical tools to mimic the randomized trial that we would have liked to perform (target trial)
-   Framework works well for interventions which you can control (pharmaceutical treatment, surgery, behavioral intervention, income, etc.) and at what time point they are delivered
-   Part of specifying target trial is the inclusion/exclusion criteria, intervention (type, intensity/dosage, timing), follow-up and outcomes
-   Framework leaves out many factors which we may be interested in (particularly race/ethnicity, gender, etc.)

## Causal Inference: Non-Target Trial

-   Causal methods are useful to create balance among certain characteristics between different groups
-   Important to think of what characteristics AT WHAT TIME POINT we want balanced
-   In other words, WHEN would you have done the randomization - Balancing on different characteristics at different time points gives insight on when differences emerge
-   For example, ER doctor looking at outcomes by race/ethnicity for those presenting with chest pain can or cannot balance on laboratory values at presentation

## Some Simple Rules

-   Which of the 4 types of variables do we want to include in regression adjustment?
-   Simulation!

```{r, echo = TRUE}
results <- NULL
num.sim <- 25
sample.size <- 30
set.seed(1101985)
for(i in 1:num.sim){
	X1 <- rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	X2 <- rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	X3 <- rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	X4 <- rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	
	#generate data
	Y1 <- 1 + X1 + X2 + rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	Y0 <- X1 + X2 + rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1)
	
	expit <- function(x) {
		expit <- exp(x)/(1+exp(x))
		return(expit)
	}
	A <- rbinom(sample.size, 1, expit(0.5*X1 + 0.5*X3))
	Y <- Y1*A + Y0*(1-A)
	observed.data <- data.frame(Y, A, X1, X2, X3, X4)
	
	m1 <- lm(Y~ A*(X4), data = observed.data)
	data_trt <- data_ctr <-observed.data
	data_trt$A = 1
	data_ctr$A = 0
	pred1 <- predict(m1, newdata = data_trt, type = "response")
	pred0 <- predict(m1, newdata = data_ctr, type = "response")
	ATE_reg <- mean(pred1 - pred0)
	
	p1 <- glm(A ~ X4, family = "binomial", data = observed.data)
	ps <- predict(p1, type = "response")
	w1 <- observed.data$A/ps
	w0 <- (1-observed.data$A)/(1-ps)
	
	ATE_IPW2 <- weighted.mean(observed.data$Y, w1) - 
	weighted.mean(observed.data$Y, w0)
	
	results <- rbind(results, c(ATE_reg, ATE_IPW2))
}
apply(results, 2, mean)
apply(results, 2, sd)
```
